subject: physics
question_text: State second law of thermodynamics. How is heat engine different from a refrigerator?

verification.note: Asked in TS March 2016 (Q21), March 2020 (Q21), March 2023 (Q21) and March 2024 (Q19) — TS Inter I-Year Physics Paper-I, Section C, 8 marks each time. The five-way mark split is INVENTED and is a CLAIM until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it. Physics hand-checked: Kelvin–Planck (no engine working in a cycle converts heat from a single reservoir entirely into work) and Clausius (heat does not flow on its own from a colder body to a hotter one) are the two equivalent statements; engine W = Q₁ − Q₂ with η = W/Q₁ = 1 − Q₂/Q₁; refrigerator Q₁ = Q₂ + W with coefficient of performance β = Q₂/W.

recall_prompt: Say the steps you would write for this answer, in order. You can speak in English, in Telugu, or in both.

steps.label: Kelvin–Planck statement
lines: The second law fixes the direction of heat
flow and limits how much heat can be turned
into work.
Kelvin–Planck statement: no engine working in
a cycle can take heat from a single reservoir
and convert all of it into work. Some heat
must be rejected to a colder body.
steps.margin_note: First mark. The words "working in a cycle" and "single reservoir" are the two checked phrases.
steps.why: The first law allows an engine that converts all its heat into work; nothing in energy conservation forbids it. The second law is the separate statement that rules it out.
common_mistakes: Leaving out "working in a cycle". A single isothermal expansion does convert all its heat into work; it is the repeated cycle that cannot.
Saying no heat can be converted into work. Part of it can; all of it cannot.

recall.must_convey: That no engine working in a cycle can take heat from a single reservoir and convert all of it into work.
accept: cannot convert all the heat into work
reject: heat cannot flow from a colder body to a hotter one

steps.memory_tip: Kelvin–Planck is about WORK: one reservoir cannot give an engine work with nothing rejected.

steps.label: Clausius statement
lines: Clausius statement: heat cannot flow on its
own from a colder body to a hotter one. It
flows that way only when external work is
done on the system.
The two statements are equivalent: if either
one were false, the other would fail as well.
steps.margin_note: Second mark. Both statements are asked, so write this one even if the first looks complete.
steps.why: Clausius covers the direction of heat flow and Kelvin–Planck covers the conversion of heat into work. Together they are what makes an engine and a refrigerator two different machines.
common_mistakes: Leaving out "on its own". Heat does flow from cold to hot in a refrigerator, because work is supplied.
Writing only one of the two statements. The question says the second law, and both statements are part of it.

recall.must_convey: That heat cannot flow on its own from a colder body to a hotter one, and does so only when external work is supplied.
accept: heat cannot flow by itself from cold to hot
reject: cannot convert all the heat into work

steps.memory_tip: Clausius is about DIRECTION: cold to hot needs work, hot to cold does not.

steps.label: The heat engine
lines: A heat engine converts heat into work in a
repeated cycle. In one cycle the working
substance takes heat Q₁ from a hot reservoir
at T₁, does external work W, and rejects heat
Q₂ to a cold reservoir at T₂.
η is always less than 1: some heat is always
rejected to the sink.
steps.margin_note: Two marks. One for the three quantities Q₁, W and Q₂ in the right places, one for the efficiency.
steps.why: The working substance returns to its starting state at the end of a cycle, so its internal energy is unchanged and the whole of Q₁ − Q₂ appears as work.
common_mistakes: Writing η = W/Q₂. The efficiency is the work divided by the heat TAKEN IN, which is Q₁.
Saying an ideal engine has η = 1. The second law forbids it; Q₂ is never zero.

recall.must_convey: That an engine takes Q one from the hot reservoir, does work W, rejects Q two to the cold reservoir, with W equal to Q one minus Q two and efficiency W by Q one.
accept: takes Q one from the source and rejects Q two to the sink
W is Q one minus Q two
efficiency is W by Q one
reject: work is done on the working substance

steps.memory_tip: Engine: Q₁ taken in, W given out, Q₂ rejected. Efficiency is W divided by Q₁.

steps.label: The refrigerator
lines: A refrigerator is the same cycle run in the
opposite direction. External work W is done
on the working substance, which takes heat Q₂
from the cold body at T₂ and rejects Q₁ to
the hot surroundings at T₁.
β can be greater than 1, so it is not called
an efficiency.
steps.margin_note: Two marks. One for work being done ON the substance and the heat moving cold to hot, one for β.
steps.why: What is wanted from a refrigerator is the heat removed from the cold body, so the useful output is Q₂ and the cost is W. That is why β is Q₂/W and not W/Q₂.
common_mistakes: Writing β = W/Q₂ upside down. The useful output Q₂ goes on top.
Calling β an efficiency. A quantity that can be greater than 1 is not called an efficiency.

recall.must_convey: That work W is done on a refrigerator, which takes Q two from the cold body and rejects Q one to the hot body, with coefficient of performance Q two by W.
accept: work is done on the refrigerator
takes Q two from the cold body
coefficient of performance is Q two by W
reject: efficiency is W by Q one

steps.memory_tip: Refrigerator: the useful output is Q₂ and the cost is W, so β = Q₂/W.

steps.label: The difference
lines: The two devices run the same cycle in
opposite directions.
Heat engine: heat flows from hot to cold on
its own and part of it is taken out as work.
Refrigerator: external work is supplied to
move heat from cold to hot, which the second
law does not allow on its own.
The engine is rated by its efficiency, the
refrigerator by its coefficient of
performance.

lines.text: Engine: η = W/Q₁ · Refrigerator: β = Q₂/W

steps.margin_note: The last two marks. One for the direction of the cycle, one for the two different performance ratios.
steps.why: The comparison is the second half of the question and is worth as much as either machine on its own, so it needs its own paragraph rather than a closing sentence.
common_mistakes: Describing both machines and never stating the difference. The question asks for the difference in so many words.
Saying a refrigerator breaks the second law. It obeys it, because external work is supplied.

recall.must_convey: That the two run the same cycle in opposite directions, the engine taking work out of a natural hot-to-cold flow and the refrigerator using supplied work to move heat cold to hot, rated by eta and beta.
accept: engine gives work, refrigerator takes work
one is rated by efficiency, the other by coefficient of performance
reject: no engine can convert all the heat into work

steps.memory_tip: Same cycle, opposite direction: the engine gives out work, the refrigerator takes work in.

insider_note: Both statements carry a mark each, so an answer with only one starts a mark down. η = W/Q₁ and β = Q₂/W carry the last two.
